catalog_quote: Our data suggest that Aʔɨwa exhibits a quantity-sensitive stress system based on right-aligned disyllabic trochees. Considering words of two to four syllables consisting solely of light syllables, as exemplified in (33) to (35), we find that words bear a single penultimate stress in words of two or three syllables, while words of four syllables exhibit primary stress in penultimate position, and a secondary stress in pre-antepenultimate position, suggesting the footing given in the cited examples. Note that the lack of secondary stresses on the leftmost syllable in three- and five-syllable forms, in (34) and (36) respectively, indicates that Aʔɨwa does not permit degenerate feet. (33) a. new_statements.quote: Our data suggest that Aʔɨwa exhibits a quantity-sensitive stress system based on right-aligned disyllabic trochees. Considering words of two to four syllables consisting solely of light syllables, as exemplified in (33) to (35), we find that words bear a single penultimate stress in words of two or three syllables, while words of four syllables exhibit primary stress in penultimate position, and a secondary stress in pre-antepenultimate position [...] Quantity sensitivity is evident in shifts from the basic trochaic pattern to an iambic pattern, when the rightmost syllable of the head is heavier the the leftmost, as in (37). Considering words of two to four syllables consisting solely of light syllables, as exemplified in (33) to (35), we find that words bear a single penultimate stress in words of two or three syllables, while words of four syllables exhibit primary stress in penultimate position, and a sec…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable (right-aligned disyllabic trochee) when the last two syllables are both light; stress shifts to the final syllable when it is heavy (closed, CVC) and the penult is light (e.g. aˈʃap, tuˈkut, akɾeˈwak). Syllables are (C)V(C); heavy = closed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the pre-antepenultimate syllable in four-syllable words, i.e. iterative right-to-left trochees ((ˌta.ha)(ˈru.ʔu) 'garden', (ˌi.sa)(ˈra.wi) 'woodpecker'; as(ˌlan.ta)(ˈni.a) 'young woman'); no secondary stress on a leftover initial syllable in 3- and 5-syllable words (no degenerate feet).
new_statements.exceptions: "a small number of exceptions.. words in which both syllables of the rightmost foot appear have the same weight, but in which the final syllable bears primary stress": haˈʔu 'basket', jaw.naˈhi 'potato sp.', hamˈham 'stingray'; authors cannot decide whether these are lexical stress or残 traces of lost contrastive vowel length. All claims explicitly tentative (two rememberers, ~160 items).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on isolated lexical items (citation forms elicited from rememberers); based on ~160 recorded words/short sentences; audio tokens archived at CLA 2019-36.004-006.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Aʔɨwa (Glottocode abis1238 stated in the chapter itself) as remembered by two rememberers (Delia Andi Macahuachi, María Estrella Clavoy) of Puerto Elvira, lower Curaray/Napo, recorded 2008-2010; ~160 lexical items and short sentences. Authors stress that all descriptive claims are tentative given extreme attrition. Same language as Tessmann's (1930) 'Auischiri' and Villarejo's (1959) 'Vacacocha'.

The image is data, not a statement, so has_stress_section 'no' is right; the marks (penultimate in light-syllable words, final when the final syllable is closed: aˈʃap, aˈkiʃ, nutˈnɨt, akɾeˈwak;…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Aʔɨwa has an empty rule; the existing statement (Beier & Michael 2023 chapter, Sec. 3.3) is weight-sensitive (right-aligned disyllabic trochees, penultimate default, heavy final syllables attract stress). The CLA Table 2 image marks exactly that pattern on the comparative wordlist, and the audio tokens are the recordings behind the chapter's Table 2 and Appendix; the archive adds no independent statement, secondary-stress claim or new exception beyond what the chapter says. Item descriptions themselves say only '32/123/30 WAV audio files of Aʔɨwa lexical items corresponding to.. Table 2.. Appendix' and '291 short WAV files of individual words, phrases, and clauses cli…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The archive bundles contain no prose about stress: they are 476 WAV tokens of single words plus one image of the chapter's Table 2. The Table 2 image marks primary stress with IPA ˈ on every polysyllabic Aʔɨwa form: penultimate in words made of light syllables (ˈsahi, wiˈʃala, wiruˈkawa, nukˈlahi, iˈkiri) and final when the last syllable is closed/heavy (aˈʃap, aˈkiʃ, nutˈnɨt, akreˈwak); disyllables with two closed syllables keep the trochee (ˈtʃahtar, ˈsikwas). This is data, not a statement; the stress marks match the quantity-sensitive right-aligned trochee analysis in Sec. 3.3 of the same authors' chapter (draft already held by the project at p. 12).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not marked in the Table 2 image (only primary ˈ); the WAV files carry no annotation. The chapter draft held by the project (Sec. 3.3, ex. 35-36) reports secondary stress on the pre-antepenult in four-syllable light words and no degenerate feet.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in the archive. In the Table 2 image, atˈku / atˈkua 'house' and nuiˈnui 'cotton' show final stress where the weight rule would not obviously predict it; the chapter draft's ex. (38) (haˈʔu, jawnaˈhi, hamˈham) already lists a small set of such final-stressed exceptions and leaves open whether they are lexical stress or relics of vowel length.
new_statements.identity_note: All material is from a single speaker, Delia Luisa Andi Macahuachi (DAM), recorded at Puerto Elvira and Iquitos, Loreto, Peru, 2008 and 2010 (CLA item metadata); the chapter draft held by the project states 'Glottocode: abis1238' on p. 1. The Table 2 image also contains Iquito, Waorani and Máíhɨ̃ki columns, which are other languages and were not used.

sources.note: Sec. 3.3 'Stress' (ms p. 12): quantity-sensitive system of right-aligned disyllabic trochees: penultimate primary stress in all-light words, secondary stress on pre-antepenult in 4-syllable words, no degenerate feet; iambic (final) stress when the final syllable is heavier than the penult (aˈʃap, tuˈkut, akɾeˈwak); a few lexical exceptions with final stress on equal-weight syllables (haˈʔu, jawnaˈhi, hamˈham).
